content.confidence: 3: You are fairly confident in your assessment. It is possible that you did not understand some parts of the submission or that you are unfamiliar with some pieces of related work. Math/other details were not carefully checked.
content.summary_of_the_paper: The authors propose to apply the tools of domain adaptation to the task of adversarially defending against unseen attacks. Concretly, they claim to show that variance-based risk extrapolation can be used to significantly improve adversarial robustness to an ensemble of attacks.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
The paper evaluates on a variety of attacks and compares to several baseline methods.

A major conceptual problem I see with this paper is that the distinction between different attacks and different threat models is very muddled. The authors say they want to achieve robustness to unseen attacks, but then they actually train and evaluate on different threat models. In principle, these two are different tasks and the authors seem to be attempting to do both while saying they want to achieve robustness to unseen attacks. I would even argue that the task of generalizing to unseen attacks of the same threat model is simply the normal task of adversarial robustness.

A more minor issue is that the authors' clean models have surprisingly low accuracy to begin with. 98% on MNIST can be explained by them using an MLP as opposed to a CNN (which they justify by wanting to have very diverse architectures). But 87.6% on CIFAR10 is much too low for a ResNet18. They say that this is before optimizing the hyperparameters but then they don't show what the optimized version would be.

I am also confused as to why they did not include the max method by Tramèr & Boneh (2019) as a baseline, given that they do discuss it.

The authors also remove some attacks from their main evaluations, seemingly just because their models performed poorly against them. They state that those attacks are "overtuned" but they don't explain what this term means.

The actual technical innovation that the authors provide (i.e. adding the variance across attacks in the loss) is very minor.

Another very minor point is that the title could potentially mislead some people, since there also exists a literature on providing adversarial robustness on out-of-distribution data.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
Despite the authors giving a nice overview of prior work, I think the paper needs major improvements in the clarity of stating its goal.

The novelty is very limited.

The authors say they provide code, but redacted it for the review period. They could have had an anonymized link or provided supplementary material, neither of which they did. Therefore, it is hard to judge the reproducibility of the work.
content.summary_of_the_review: The paper's contribution is not presented very clearly and does not appear particularly impactful. In my opinion, given that there are no theoretical or technical innovations, the empirical results do not warrant a publication at ICLR.

content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.

content.title: Part 1/2 of initial reply
content.comment:
> A major conceptual problem I see with this paper is that the distinction between different attacks and different threat models is very muddled. The authors say they want to achieve robustness to unseen attacks, but then they actually train and evaluate on different threat models. In principle, these two are different tasks and the authors seem to be attempting to do both while saying they want to achieve robustness to unseen attacks

As stated in the paper/methodology: the threat model is whitebox gradient-based attack with the inclusion of AutoAttack which is not purely gradient-based whitebox. Within that threat model exist different attacks. Experimental evaluations can only evaluate on so many attacks, and some of those attacks do not even exist yet, but may be invented after defenses are designed  (the so-called cat and mouse game of adversarial ML). Therefore, within that threat model, accuracy on individual attacks does not capture robustness. Robustness is the accuracy on the ensemble of all attacks of the threat model. This is biased by the strongest performing attacks, which often are attacks not trained on. So we use unseen attacks in our ensemble to estimate the actual robustness on the threat model, since as argued in our literature background section, those tend to be the problem. If we are able to generalise to unseen attacks within the threat model, we may hope that our model is generally more robust given the threat model. This is really the same argument as why domain generalisation evaluates on specific unseen domains at test time: they are just estimating the performance on any unseen domain the model might realistically be used on after being deployed. 

> I would even argue that the task of generalizing to unseen attacks of the same threat model is simply the normal task of adversarial robustness.

We agree with the reviewer. As explained, unseen attacks within a threat model allow us to simulate performance against novel types of attacks / distributional shifts. Even within single-perturbation robustness work, authors generally (are encouraged to) evaluate on other attacks that the one they trained on. Perhaps the author is pointing out that this nomenclature is highlighted in our work more than usual – aside from the reasons given so far, it is also to emphasise the connection with domain generalisation for readers interested or familiar with that area of machine learning.

> A more minor issue is that the authors' clean models have surprisingly low accuracy to begin with. 98% on MNIST can be explained by them using an MLP as opposed to a CNN (which they justify by wanting to have very diverse architectures). But 87.6% on CIFAR10 is much too low for a ResNet18. They say that this is before optimizing the hyperparameters but then they don't show what the optimized version would be.

Perhaps the reviewer is thinking of work such as https://arxiv.org/pdf/2206.13424v3.pdf achieving 95% accuracy (the highest on paperswithcode), but note that this is achieved through several techniques that are not considered here or relevant to our claims, such as data augmentation. That being said, with hyperparameter optimisation, we find a clean accuracy of 92.7%. 

> I am also confused as to why they did not include the max method by Tramèr & Boneh (2019) as a baseline, given that they do discuss it.

Tables 3 and 4 of Maini et al. do evaluate on many individual attacks that were not seen during training https://arxiv.org/pdf/1909.04068.pdf. Note that Maini et al. find on CIFAR10 that Avg performs significantly better than Max. Moreover, on both MNIST and CIFAR10, Maini et al find that MSD performs better than both Avg and Max anyway, so improving on MSD with REx suggests that MSD+REx would outperform Max on both datasets. 

However, a significant difference with Maini is that we use different tunings for some attacks, and as evidenced by several reviewers asking for it, it would be valuable to readers of the paper that we add this baseline.

content.title: Rebuttal unconvincing
content.comment:
I acknowledge the authors' rebuttal and appreciate their thorough response.

Unfortunately, I find their arguments unconvincing. According to their clarification they really mostly care about domain generalization in the sense of robustness within the same threat model but using different attacks. If that's the case then they should separately evaluate the different threat models, which they instead all join in their evaluation. As I stated in my original review, this causes unnecessary confusion by conflating two very different concepts, and their rebuttal has not sufficiently addressed this.

I also agree with Reviewer S482 that there is not a lot of value in providing robustness against weak attack.

> We already specify, just below table 1 in our discussion, “overtuned (i.e. tuned too strongly, leading to negligible accuracy)”. 

That's just not true. The term is used there but definitely not explained. The revision period could have been used to address issues such as this.

> We only remove them from the ensembles for all models because no model performs well on them so they push down the ensemble accuracy close to 0-3%, limiting the signal. 

In that case that should be openly stated and discussed. At any rate, if no model can solve the task that the authors set for themselves, I don't see how they can make any claim about their model being "better" than the others. Unless they want to argue that their task involving a cherry-picked subset of threat models is somehow inherently interesting, in which case, why did they not pick this subset to begin with?

Overall, I do not see a path for this paper to overcome its deficits without undergoing very major revisions in terms of scope and methodology.

Yes, as Tramer et al., which use existing approaches of Average and Max, ours lies in the empirical novelty. While the variance as a regulariser is an old mathematical trick, it is really unclear why the reviewer considers the empirical novelty or significance to be marginal, when our work provides significant improvements on existing approaches evaluated, on an evaluation similar to that of existing literature in that area, based on an approach never attempted to the best of our knowledge in adversarial machine learning.

content.confidence: 5: You are absolutely certain about your assessment. You are very familiar with the related work and checked the math/other details carefully.
content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper proposes to improve the robustness of classifiers against multiple, and possibly unseen, adversarial attacks thanks to a domain generalization perspective: each attack used at training time is considered a separate domain, and the Risk Extrapolation method (REx) is used to improve worst-case robustness. In the experimental evaluation on MNIST and CIFAR-10, the proposed approach can improve the performance of commonly used methods for robustness in multiple $\ell_p$-threat models.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths
- The motivation for using REx is reasonable, and the method in practice requires small modifications to the existing training schemes.

- In the experimental evaluation, it seems that both Avg and MSD benefit from the combination with REx.

Weaknesses
- The experimental setup seems a bit confusing. First, using stronger attacks in the same threat model, e.g. increasing the number of iterations in CW or using AutoAttack instead of PGD, does not constitute a new domain since, as mentioned in the paper, the robustness in a given threat model should be evaluated as the worst-case among the various available methods. Also, reporting the robust accuracy of an unbounded attack like CW (as it seems to be used in the experiments) is problematic to interpret, since in principle it should drop to 0% if sufficiently many iterations are allowed and unless there is some form of gradient obfuscation. Finally, the choice of performing most of the experiments with a suboptimal training scheme (fixed learning rate, no weight decay) is unusual, and different methods might interact differently with such scheme.

- There is no comparison to the Max method, which should perform better than Avg for robustness to multiple $\ell_p$-attacks.

- The parameters used for the attacks $P_1$ and $P_2$, reported in the appendix, seems suboptimal, especially for CIFAR-10, since the  step size is very small compared to the value of $\epsilon$. Also, no stronger attack for the $\ell_1$-threat model is used, and $P_1$ might be not very effective since all models, even those not trained with it, show high robustness to it.

- The epoch at which REx is activated varies and is optimized for each case individually.

- The presentation of the results is hard to follow, since the parameters of the attacks, in particular the values of $\epsilon$, are not reported in the main part and change across methods. Also, the set of attacks used for each experiment is not consistent.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
Clarity: the notation is often used without being first introduced, and, as mentioned above, the presentation of the results can be improved.

Quality: the proposed method seems to improve existing methods, but I think that the current evaluation is not sufficient.

Novelty: the paper does not propose a new algorithm, but applies REx to a different task.

Reproducibility: the paper contains many details about the experimental setup. However, the epoch at which the REx penalty is activated seems to be tuned for each case, which might make REx difficult to use.
content.summary_of_the_review: While the proposed method might be interesting, the experimental evaluation is currently not sufficiently clear, as it misses well defined threat models and some baseline. Clarity of the presentation, especially of the results, might be improved.

replying_to: Replying to Official Review of Paper5742 by Reviewer z5Zx

content.title: Part 1/3 of initial reply
content.comment:
> First, using stronger attacks in the same threat model, e.g. increasing the number of iterations in CW or using AutoAttack instead of PGD, does not constitute a new domain since, as mentioned in the paper, the robustness in a given threat model should be evaluated as the worst-case among the various available methods. 

We believe that there is indeed confusion here. The holy grail of adversarial machine learning would indeed be robustness against all attacks, which implies that an ensemble of all attacks would not be able to successfully fool the model (within reason of course as otherwise we may get trivially strong perturbations. While a common characterisation of “within reason” has been the use of standardised hyperparameter choices and enforcing Lp norm bounds, we relax it here into “as long as there is a signal with any defense” meaning neither 0 nor 100% accuracy). However, in the absence of access to all attacks and with more realistic aspirations, we typically train and evaluate on a limited number of attacks. 
1. A somewhat inevitable flaw in this methodology is the cat and mouse game it induces: as improvements are made on some attacks, new attacks are designed to overcome them.
2. Moreover, in practice, the choice of tuning of attacks is arbitrary – attackers are not obligated to use $\epsilon = 8/255$ or any other hyperparameter tuning of the attacks. The only constraint for an attacker is to be able to evade detection in practice, and such detection may not even be implemented! Therefore, models should also be robust to different choices of tunings of the same attacks used during training.

In the threat model we define, an attacker is free to use any white box gradient-based attack, with any tuning they want. They are not constrained by epsilon or any other hyperparameter, albeit we are for obvious methodological reasons (we need to be able to implement something after all). In the line of defenses we improve, adversarial training is used on a choice of attacks. Similarly to them, we have access to some attacks during training, which we refer to as the seen attacks in the paper. Ideally, to perform well on the entire threat model defined, that is, on an ensemble of all attacks in that threat model, we would need to perform well on every single one of them. But there are infinitely many such attacks, factoring in tuning, so we can only evaluate on a selection of unseen attacks. By having entirely unseen attacks, and unseen tunings of some of the seen attacks, we attempt to cover points 1. and 2. to highlight that we get improvements on both kinds of distributional shifts if they induce strong attacks. In turn, such strong attacks capture the ensemble performance metric, so improving on each such domain leads to an improvement on the ensemble. This is similar enough to the domain generalisation setting: ideally, we want generalisation to any possible realistic domain, but we have to evaluate on a select few unseen domains at test time to estimate the performance on any unseen domain. In that case however, the setup would not allow as in adversarial machine learning to use the same ensemble metric (which as a reminder, is mean over unperturbed data of minimum over domains of performance).

In a nutshell, they’re new domains because they correspond to different distributional shifts, and the relationship with the worst-case ensemble performance is that these individual domains are used to compute the worst-case performance, and to track how REx affects performance given 1. and 2. See first part of discussion with reviewer S482 for more details.


> Also, reporting the robust accuracy of an unbounded attack like CW (as it seems to be used in the experiments) is problematic to interpret, since in principle it should drop to 0% if sufficiently many iterations are allowed and unless there is some form of gradient obfuscation.

The reviewer is correct – it is the choice of hyperparameters in CW and its stopping mechanic in the Borealis AI Advertorch implementation that allow us to get a non-trivial accuracy on each dataset. The modified tuning of CW does run into this issue on CIFAR10, suggesting an absence of gradient obfuscation (as we mention, this is why we still report that figure). We did run an experiment that we will add in the appendix where we reject adversarial examples that leave the L2 eps = 0.5 bound on CIFAR10 (to use the limit of PGD L2 which uses the same p norm) on the hyperparameter-optimised models. Our findings are the following:
1. Avg: 28.7% accuracy
2. Avg+REx: 43.0% accuracy
3. MSD: 32.9% accuracy
4. MSD+REx: 34.1% accuracy
While REx still provides an improvement, we note that our intent, as explained in the previous point, is to simulate an attacker that is free to use any attack in the threat model within reason, which our tuning of unbounded CW is a part of, and which still serves to show an advantage in using REx.

content.title: Part 2/3 of initial reply
content.comment:
> Finally, the choice of performing most of the experiments with a suboptimal training scheme (fixed learning rate, no weight decay) is unusual, and different methods might interact differently with such scheme.

We fail to see how this is a weakness: we provide both results for a non-hyperparameter-optimised and an individually hyperparameter-optimised training scheme in respectively 4.2 and 4.4. If anything, we precisely explore how the hyperparameter-optimisation affects the advantage in using REx vs not doing hyperparameter-optimisation as we provide both sets of results. That was the point: since it may affect the relative performance when using REx, we do both. And indeed, it did affect the relative advantage in using REx as discussed in 4.4 since it reduces the relative improvement in using REx over MSD. It also shows that using REx naively without attempting hyperparameter tuning instead of hyperparameter-tuning MSD without REx, which can be computationally expensive, leads to fairly similar ensemble performance at a fraction of the computational time. On individual attacks, the same argument holds when comparing optimised Avg and non-optimised Avg+REx.

> There is no comparison to the Max method, which should perform better than Avg

Tables 3 and 4 of Maini et al. do evaluate on many individual attacks that were not seen during training https://arxiv.org/pdf/1909.04068.pdf. Note that Maini et al. find on CIFAR10 that Avg performs significantly better than Max. Moreover, on both MNIST and CIFAR10, Maini et al find that MSD performs better than both Avg and Max anyway, so improving on MSD with REx suggests that MSD+REx would outperform Max on both datasets. 

However, a significant difference with Maini is that we use different tunings for some attacks, and as evidenced by several reviewers asking for it, it would be valuable to readers of the paper that we add this baseline.

> Tuning of P1 and P2

There is no “optimal” tuning per se of attacks as explained in the first point of our rebuttal to the reviewer, but we understand the point they are making. The step size vs epsilon, however, is unlikely to have a significant effect, because PGD attacks in our and most implementations initialise randomly within the epsilon ball for a given sample. The concern about step size vs epsilon would be very true if PGD attacks started at the unperturbed datapoint and did not perform this random initialisation step. In our experience changing the step size had no significant effect, as evidenced by our use of another set of tuning for those on CIFAR10 in 4.4 (see Appendix A.1), inspired by Rice et al. 2020.

>  no stronger attack for the l1-threat model is used

We do not insist on L1 because our threat model is not a specific p-norm, it is the one defined in the methodology section, which is agnostic to the choice of p-norm. If our work was concerned with generalising within L1 bounded attacks we would use more attacks. Here, we already have a lot of attacks, and the L1 attack is merely here to show generalisation (or lack thereof) to a potentially unseen norm. In general, we believe the community is mostly focused on Linf and to a lesser extent L2 norm attacks among the Lp gradient-based white box attacks.

content.title: Part 3/3 of initial reply
content.comment:
> The epoch at which REx is activated varies and is optimized for each case individually. 
> Reproducibility: the paper contains many details about the experimental setup. However, the epoch at which the REx penalty is activated seems to be tuned for each case, which might make REx difficult to use.

As argued in the appendix and the main body of the paper, in every setting except for [MSD + REx on CIFAR10 in the hyperparameter optimised case] (only one of 8 of our REx model evaluations !), activating REx at any time appears to lead to improvements. So we do not believe this to be a weakness in general. It is true however, as we discuss in the paper, that it did require multiple attempts in the [MSD + REx on CIFAR10 in the hyperparameter optimised case]. We explain this in the paper by the fact that regularising by the variance over multiple domains (REx) is originally designed to be used in conjunction with ERM (equivalently Avg) on those domains. Note that for critical applications, this search is not costly enough to disregard the adversarial robustness advantage in using REx. 
In a nutshell, REx only required efforts searching for a starting epoch in a single modality out of 8, a modality on which REx was not expected to work, and which it still managed to improve. 

Perhaps we will add in the appendix a short description of what happens with “bad” choices of starting epoch: such a REx model achieves higher worst-case ensemble performance (all) by a slightly superior amount than the “good” MSD+REx model due to performing even better on CW (up to 3% based on how “bad”), but a relatively similar (slightly better or worse depending on how “bad”, within 0.5%) ensemble seen (so PGD Linf L2 L1) performance than MSD on its own. Therefore, then again, in the 1 in 8 setting where REx requires some care, not being careful enough still does not really harm the performance. The reviewer may wonder why such results are not included: we wanted to simulate not having access to unseen attacks at all during model selection, and only base our choices on the seen ensembles. Otherwise, unseen attacks would not be truly unseen from a methodological point of view. As such, “good” choices are defined by finding a good enough improvement in seen ensembles, and “bad” ensembles may actually not be bad once unseen attacks are factored in.

> The presentation of the results is hard to follow, since the parameters of the attacks [...] are not reported in the main part and change across methods. 

Since this is a multi-perturbation robustness paper that varies tuning even within a choice of attacks, we believe this is best left to the appendix as it would overload the main body of the paper and confuse readers. Just to clarify, the tuning changes between datasets, and then slight changes are made on PGD L1 and L2 in the hyperparameter-optimised case (there is also a reduction in the number of iterations of PGD Linf, which is known not to affect ResNet18 on CIFAR10). Everything is indicated clearly in appendix A.1. We will add a hyperlink however between the relevant sections of 4.1, 4.2, 4.4 and appendix A.1 as we understand that scrolling back and forth can be quite inconvenient.

> Quality: the proposed method seems to improve existing methods, but I think that the current evaluation is not sufficient.

Could the reviewer details how the current evaluation is insufficient, especially compared to that of existing literature on the same research problem (multi-perturbation robustness) ?

> Empirical Novelty And Significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.

While the variance as a regulariser is an old mathematical trick, it is really unclear why the reviewer considers the empirical novelty or significance to be marginal, when our work provides significant improvements on existing approaches evaluated, on an evaluation similar to that of existing literature in that area, based on an approach never attempted to the best of our knowledge in adversarial machine learning.

content.confidence: 5: You are absolutely certain about your assessment. You are very familiar with the related work and checked the math/other details carefully.
content.summary_of_the_paper: While there has been plenty of work over the years on addressing the robustness of neural networks against single perturbation types, significantly less work exists on training models robust against multiple perturbations types. This is essential as it is known that models robust against one type of perturbation are not necessarily robust against others. The authors of this paper try to address this issue by applying the method of variance-based risk extrapolation (REx). Evaluation is performed on the popular MNIST and CIFAR10 datasets showing improved empirical robustness against multiple norm-based perturbations than prior methods based on adversarial training.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:
1. Generating networks robust against multiple robustness types is harder than the single perturbation robustness considered by most existing works. The problem considered here is therefore important and challenging. 

2. The idea of formulating robustness as a domain generalization problem is interesting.

Weaknesses:
1. The technical ideas are shallow and involve simply changing the loss function. This could be acceptable for ICRL if the authors provide theoretical insights into why adding the extra variance term should lead to better generalization. However, no theoretical studies are provided.

2. The experimental evaluation is not convincing (more on this below).

3. The paper is not well-written and often uses terms/symbols not defined in the paper.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
Clarity: The title of the paper is a bit misleading as it does not tackle out-of-distribution robustness. The norm-based perturbations create images within the local neighborhood of examples in the test set, therefore all generated images are still in distribution. Also, it is not clear whether the method is limited to handling norm-based perturbations or also applies to semantic perturbations (e.g., https://proceedings.neurips.cc/paper/2019/file/f7fa6aca028e7ff4ef62d75ed025fe76-Paper.pdf, https://openaccess.thecvf.com/content_CVPR_2020/papers/Mohapatra_Towards_Verifying_Robustness_of_Neural_Networks_Against_A_Family_of_CVPR_2020_paper.pdf).

The authors often use symbols/terms that are undefined which could make the concepts inaccessible to an unfamiliar reader. For example, in eq. (3)-(6), "x" is undefined and it is not clear what is the distribution for computing the expectation (although I can imagine it is wrt images in the distribution of the classifier). In Section 3, the set {MSD} is undefined. In the Tables, I did not find any detail about how the robustness for the rows with ensembles was computed. 

I find referring to C&W, PGD, and DeepFool attacks as different domains confusing. These create examples within the same type of perturbation model and therefore should be considered instances of the same domain.

Quality: In Section 2.2, the authors mention that ", a key difference with most work in domain generalization, is that when adversarially training, the training distribution shifts every epoch, as the attacks are computed from the continuously updated values of the weights." This is indeed true and the main challenge here but their solution does not address it. I am not sure why they mention it. 

The MNIST classifier used in Section 4 is quite small and therefore suited for formal verification. I see no reason why the robustness should be measured by running attacks when formal proof of robustness is possible. The authors should try running one of the state-of-the-art complete verifiers (https://github.com/Verified-Intelligence/alpha-beta-CROWN, https://github.com/eth-sri/eran, https://github.com/NeuralNetworkVerification/Marabou) to make the evaluation results more convincing and also simplify the presentation of the evaluation which is currently quite cluttered. Without formal analysis, the current evaluation will also lead to a game of cat and mouse where subsequent papers may break the robustness of the networks presented here by finding stronger attacks.

The verifiers are also able to find adversarial examples that the attacks considered in this paper cannot (see https://proceedings.mlr.press/v162/zhang22ae/zhang22ae.pdf). The authors should consider running these attacks for the CIFAR10 ResNet18 network in case the proof of properties does not scale. If possible, the authors can also consider training a smaller network with their method and run formal verification to prove that their method can generate formally robust models for CIFAR10 as well.

Novelty: I did not find enough technical depth here to merit a publication at ICLR. The authors could consider fixing the weights of intermediate layers during training (see https://openreview.net/forum?id=SJxSDxrKDr) for handling the second challenge listed in Section 2.2 to add algorithmic contributions. They should also try providing theoretical insights (e.g., modeling the effect of adding variance add to the average loss) into the workings of their method to make the technical contributions more appealing. 

Reproducibility: The reproducibility statement is adequate for ICLR.
content.summary_of_the_review: In summary, the paper handles a relatively less explored but important and hard problem. The high-level idea of connecting robustness and domain generalization is interesting however, the technical novelty, presentation, and evaluation in the current form are not sufficient to deserve acceptance at ICLR.
content.correctness: 2: Several of the paper’s claims are incorrect or not well-supported.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.
content.empirical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.

replying_to: Replying to Official Review of Paper5742 by Reviewer dbeL

content.title: Part 1/2 of initial reply
content.comment:
> The technical ideas are shallow and involve simply changing the loss function. This could be acceptable for ICRL if the authors provide theoretical insights into why adding the extra variance term should lead to better generalization. However, no theoretical studies are provided. 
> [Novelty paragraph about not enough depth]

Respectfully, we invite reviewers to evaluate how well supported our claims are by our methodology, and whether a similar combination of claims and methodology has been proposed before. To the best of our knowledge, our work is the first in proposing to use REx in a domain generalisation formulation to defend against one or multiple adversarial perturbations, and achieves great success on the same methodology/benchmarks multi-robustness papers typically use. 

While we agree that theory would have been a valuable addition, we make no claims of theory and propose an empirical evaluation of our claims. Past work in defending against multiple perturbations, a research question the reviewer acknowledges to be challenging yet much necessary, does not necessarily propose theory – see for example the MSD paper (Maini et al. 2020). 

Note that while the original REx paper presents some general motivation for domain generalisation approaches based on causality, it does not propose a theory for how specifically the variance leads to better generalisation. We are not aware of any work that has proposed a theory for variance-REx in the stationary case of domain generalisation. Moreover, our proposal considers a non-stationary case (domains shift every weight update since attacks are computed from the current value of the weights), which generally presents very significant additional challenges. Therefore, in light of the absence of theory in the conceptually simpler domain generalisation setting, we believe that requiring theory here would be unreasonable.

> Clarity: The title of the paper is a bit misleading as it does not tackle out-of-distribution robustness. The norm-based perturbations create images within the local neighborhood of examples in the test set, therefore all generated images are still in distribution.

We respectfully disagree with the reviewer on this statement. The reviewer seems to be claiming that norm-based perturbations are in-distribution with one another or even with the test set. We invite the reviewer to read the first point of our discussion with reviewer S482. At a very high level, they are all adversarial attacks, but the use of different attacks or tuning will lead to different spaces being explored even if the constraint set (Lp ball) was the same. As “proof” by contradiction, if different attacks generated the same domain (i.e. they are sampling the same distribution),  standard statistical learning theory results under i.i.d. assumptions would imply that the performance across domains would be the same/similar. 

Perhaps the reviewer means that we already train on some of the domains we evaluate on. This is correct for some of them, especially considering that splitting a dataset between training, validation and testing sets will not yield distributions with significant shifts between each other. However, we specifically describe how some attacks or tunings of attacks have not been seen at all during training. These represent novel types of distributional shifts at test time until proven otherwise. Once again, if any two domains truly were in-distribution of one another, i.i.d. results would imply we would see the same performance on both on average. This is evidently not the case in our results.

> Also, it is not clear whether the method is limited to handling norm-based perturbations or also applies to semantic perturbations

Our threat model is similar to that widely used in the past work on robustness against multiple perturbations (see the methodology of all references in our paper). We explicitly state in the methodology section that “In this work, we consider white-box attacks, which are typically the strongest type of attacks as they assume the attacker has access to the model and its parameters. Additionally, the attacks considered in the evaluations are gradient-based, with the exception of AutoAttack, which is composite and includes gradient-free perturbations”. We have not considered semantic perturbations as they are concerned with different problems, and multi-perturbation robustness in the setting we study is still an open problem. We thank the reviewers for inviting us to clarify this, and will specify in the paper that we are concerned with norm-based perturbations.

> eq. (3)-(6), "x" is undefined and it is not clear what is the distribution for computing the expectation (although I can imagine it is wrt images in the distribution of the classifier)


We thank the reviewer for pointing this out and will fix this.

replying_to: Replying to Part 1/2 of initial reply

content.title: Re: claims about out-of-distribution
content.comment:
Dear Authors,

Thanks for your response.  I believe your characterization of what constitutes an out-of-distribution example is not correct. Your arguments and "proofs" above assume that if one classifier performs badly for some distribution of examples (either benign or adversarial), then these points are out of distribution for "all" classifiers that can be trained on the dataset.  First, in a non-adversarial setting, I can train deliberately train a "bad" classifier that performs well on training data but misclassifies points in the test set. If one considers an adversarial setting, then the distribution of adversarial examples depends on the classifier, the attack algorithm, and its hyperparameters.  Indeed, the provable defense line of work can obtain classifiers with no adversarial examples within norm-based regions but the classifiers lose accuracy on test data. As per your arguments, now these test points are out-of-distribution. The definition of what constitutes an in or out-of-distribution example is independent of the classifier. Coupling it with the exact classifier, attack algorithm, etc is meaningless. The point of adversarial example generation is to expose vulnerabilities within in-distribution and motivate the training of classifiers that are robust and accurate. 

Overall, I believe that this research direction is interesting and the work has promise. I encourage the authors to better scope their work and improve contributions in the next iteration of this paper.

replying_to: Replying to Official Review of Paper5742 by Reviewer dbeL

content.title: Part 2/2 of initial reply
content.comment:
> In Section 3, the set {MSD} is undefined.

MSD is defined in bold page 3 of the manuscript and accompanied by a footnote.

>  In the Tables, I did not find any detail about how the robustness for the rows with ensembles was computed.

The description can be found in the first paragraph of the Methodology (“Threat model”), and in equation 5. It is the same as in other work on multi-perturbation robustness and Athalye et al. 2018.


> I find referring to C&W, PGD, and DeepFool attacks as different domains confusing. These create examples within the same type of perturbation model and therefore should be considered instances of the same domain.

Respectfully, we disagree with the reviewer's perspective on the relation between adversarial attacks and domains given their conventional definition. As stated when addressing a previous point, we invite the reviewer to see our discussion with reviewer S482, that we will incorporate in the appendix. They would be the same domain if they were drawn from the same distribution. As a reminder: if that were true, and those domains were in-distribution, standard i.i.d. results would imply that the same performance would be observed on average on the different domains. In general two quantities are not equal until proven otherwise. We are aware of no such result in the literature, and as argued, it is reasonably empirically suggested not to be true by all adversarial ML papers finding differences in performance on different attacks. Some reasons for the distributional shifts can be found in our discussion with reviewer S482, and will be added in the aforementioned new appendix section.

> Suggestion to use verifiers

Re: “clutter”, 
1. Our paper and methodology are designed to support, among others, the claim that the advantage in using REx is not just on a single particular dataset. Therefore, the “cluttered” way of evaluating (in the sense of running all those evaluations on MNIST) is much needed to verify that claim, as it allows readers to compare the performance with and without REx on two different datasets. Replacing only the MNIST evaluation with a formal verification would prevent us from making those claims. 
2. From a root cause analysis point of view, it was also important to test the interaction of the combination of factors {REx AND individual hyperparameter optimisation}, which led to two evaluations on CIFAR10. It highlights that the advantage in using REx is not only due to how we perform our hyperparameter optimisation, and that an advantage can be observed even when not performing hyperparameter optimisation, on two datasets, and that this ensemble performance also reflects improvements on individual attacks. 
3. Moreover, most of the literature in the area of research we are concerned with (as evidenced by the methodology of most if not all of the papers we cite) still focuses on similar attacks in their evals. Thus, those can be compared directly to our results (for example, a reader interested in only PGD Linf robustness may see that our results in the hyperparameter-optimised case suggest training on multiple domains with MSD+REx could help achieve better accuracy on PGD Linf than just training on PGD Linf). Such individual attacks can be transferred even if the attacker does not have access to the model, and our methodology allows us to understand against which common attack our model is weakest (in the white-box attack setting, which is a worst-case evaluation from the defense’s point of view). 
4. Finally, formal verification would anyway correspond to a different threat model than the one we specify and therefore would completely change the nature of our paper. See Athalye et al. 2018 for a strong argument why authors should keep their claims restricted to a threat model they clearly define. 

However, we hope the lack of formal verification, while an interesting suggestion we will consider, was not a criterion for rejection for the reviewer. Indeed, we strongly disbelieve the opinion to require it is representative of the adversarial machine learning community at large, and as argued, is not required by the scientific method given our claims. Verifiers have also not been used in the line of work we make references to, and that our work builds upon and can be compared to thanks to the methodology used.


> Empirical Novelty And Significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.

While the variance as a regulariser is an old mathematical trick, it is really unclear why the reviewer considers the empirical novelty or significance to be marginal, when our work provides significant improvements on existing approaches evaluated, on an evaluation no less rigorous than the existing literature in that area, based on an approach never attempted to the best of our knowledge in adversarial machine learning.

content.confidence: 4: You are confident in your assessment, but not absolutely certain. It is unlikely, but not impossible, that you did not understand some parts of the submission or that you are unfamiliar with some pieces of related work.
content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper connects the areas of domain generalization and adversarial robustness, proposing to use Risk Extrapolation (REx) to improve generalization of adversarial defenses against unseen attacks. The REx method involves minimizing the mean loss of a classifier against a set of attacks plus a penalty term that consists of the variance of losses against those attacks. The authors apply REx to training classifiers on MNIST and CIFAR-10 with various sets of training attacks. They compare to baselines of training against a single attack as well as MSD and using the average of the losses without the penalty term. On CIFAR-10, while their defense generally reduces accuracy against some easier attacks, it increases the accuracy against more difficult ones and thus the overall ensemble accuracy.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
I think in general the paper is promising. The approach is well-motivated, the results seem good, the writing clearly describes the method and experiments, and the appendices provide additional details as needed.

I do have some suggestions about the presentation and evaluation that I encourage the authors to consider:

 * First, generalizing to unseen attacks is a bit of an overloaded term. In this paper, "unseen" seems to refer to (i) attacks using a different optimizer (e.g., DeepFool vs. PGD), (ii) attacks at a different bound (e.g, $L_\infty$ with $\epsilon = 8/255$ vs. $\epsilon = 12/255$), and (iii) attacks with a different norm entirely, (e.g., $L_\infty$ vs. $L_1$). I think that in general (i) is not so interesting, since basically all good adversarial robustness papers already train against a cheap attack (e.g., PGD with 10 steps) and evaluate against a the strongest attack or ensemble of attacks they can find (e.g., AutoAttack). In fact, Figure 1 seems misleading to me since it suggests that the optimization method of C&W is somehow breaking the PGD-based defense, whereas as far as I can tell this is actually due to the C&W attack using a larger norm bound. I would clarify this. It would also be good to generally make this distinction between different kinds of generalization to unseen attacks, and which experiments show which types of generalization. For instance, training on $\mathcal{D}$ and testing on $P_1$ seems to be the only experiment showing type (iii) of generalizing to a new norm. The other experiments mainly seem to test (i) and (ii).
 * On a related note, if you want to test defenses against a larger norm bound (e.g., as in the $P_\infty^\bullet$ and $\text{CW}_2^\bullet$ attacks), why not use the strongest attack you can at that bound, which is AutoAttack? Restricting to evaluating against PGD at the larger $L_\infty$ bound and C&W at the larger $L_2$ bound seems a bit strange, since AutoAttack is stronger than both.
 * Finally, there are some more natural baselines that the authors could compare against. I don't think all of these are necessary to evaluate, but following my first bullet point the authors should clearly state what types of generalization to unseen attacks they are claiming and then consider which baselines are making similar claims. 
    - The Max method from Tramèr and Boneh. I know MSD is supposedly better than Max, but this was only evaluated against the attack norms seen during training in Maini et al. It's possible Max does better than MSD against unseen attacks.
    - Perceptual Adversarial Training [1], which was designed to transfer to novel threat models.
    - Larger-bound PGD adversarial training. In the results of [2], it seems like training against $L_2$ attacks at a larger bound, for instance, transfers better to unseen attacks.


[1] Laidlaw et al. Perceptual adversarial robustness: Defense against unseen threat models. ICLR 2020.
[2] Kang et al. Testing Robustness Against Unforeseen Adversaries.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The paper is clear and the quality seems good, with most best-practices for adversarial evaluation being followed and plenty of details for reproducibility. I was a bit disappointed that the authors didn't provide code for review but I they do promise it when the paper is published. The idea is a straightforward application of REx to adversarial robustness, which while not being entirely novel seems like an interesting combination of ideas to me.
content.summary_of_the_review: Overall, my impression of the paper is positive. I do think the presentation of the paper would be improved if the authors gave more clarity about the precise type of generalization to unseen attacks that they aim to improve. Then, the evaluation and baselines can be tailored to this goal. If the presentation and evaluation can be improved based on some of the feedback I have given, I would be happy to support this paper for publication at ICLR.

replying_to: Replying to Official Review of Paper5742 by Reviewer S482

content.title: Part 1/2 of initial reply
content.comment:
> First, generalizing to unseen attacks is a bit of an overloaded term. 

We thank the reviewer for their encouraging review and bringing this up. Indeed there are several factors of variability. 
1. The optimiser used: depending on the choice of optimisation algorithm or tuning of the optimiser, this will affect solutions, as is the case in general in machine learning when optimising weights. Note that here we define optimiser as optimisation algorithm.
2. The constraint for a specific p-norm
3. The choice of p-norm itself
4. The optimisation problem being solved (e.g. Carlini Wagner attacks do not optimise the same loss as the other attacks)

We respectfully disagree that variations along factors  1 and 4 do not present interesting modes of generalisation. In fact, to reuse the example of DeepFool (DF) vs PGD vs AutoAttack, we believe there would be no point in using the attacks on which the model performs best only if performance evaluations against the “strongest” attack fully captured the relative performance against the weaker attacks. This is not the case as shown in our evaluations. Indeed, taking Avg on PGDs vs REx+Avg on PGDs from Table-2, we see that while performance improves significantly on AutoAttack and PGD, it decreases to a lesser extent on DF. Therefore, AutoAttack is not sufficient in that case to fully capture the effect of using REx for each individual, “weaker” attack. 

A possible question could be “The paper argues for focusing on the worst-case ensemble performance. So does that individual performance matter for the ‘weaker’ attacks ?” This is correct – it’s unlikely for instance that DeepFool could have significantly affected the ensemble performance given its already high performance. However, we believe this could still be informative for several reasons:
1. It highlights the very fact that improving performance on a “stronger” attack is not in general synonymous with improving performance on the “weaker” attacks.
2. A reader might define their threat model more specifically than us (for example a single attack that is fast to compute), in which case they may find it useful to see whether this particular approach can be useful to them. In fact, our experiments do show that the multi-perturbation approach can help on a single attack (see Table 3 $P_\infty$ adversarial training performance vs multi-perturbation REx performance on $P_\infty$). While we make no strong claim about this in our paper, this would not be surprising, as it naturally corresponds to the notion of “positive transfer” in other machine learning areas. In a nutshell, that phenomenon describes how training on multiple data distributions can improve the performance on the individual data distributions (see for example Wu et al. 2020 https://arxiv.org/abs/2005.00944 for more info on this).

> In fact, Figure 1 seems misleading to me since it suggests that the optimization method of C&W is somehow breaking the PGD-based defense, whereas as far as I can tell this is actually due to the C&W attack using a larger norm bound

We believe C&W is indeed breaking the L2 PGD-based defense (just in case, we bring attention to the fact that it’s PGD L2 on that Figure). Two small points, for completeness: first, the learning rate decay changes the trend on the CW curve seen in that figure; second, it is not merely due to the unboundedness. Indeed, picking a hyperparameter-optimised L2 model (so including a learning rate decay) and evaluating it on CW L2 attacks where out of bound candidates are rejected (the bound is the L2 ball with $\epsilon = 0.5$ like PGD L2), the model only achieves 12.4% accuracy. As always, tuning of attacks matters, and our tuning for CW is likely the reason for this.

> [re:attacks picked to have a stronger tuning] why not use the strongest attack you can at that bound, which is AutoAttack?

We wanted to illustrate variability between potentially seen and unseen tunings of the same attack. We could add an additional AutoAttack evaluation indeed, although since AutoAttack is always unseen, it would not illustrate that point.

replying_to: Replying to Part 1/2 of initial reply
display_title: Still not convinced that performance against weaker optimization methods is so useful

content.title: Still not convinced that performance against weaker optimization methods is so useful
content.comment:
> we believe there would be no point in using the attacks on which the model performs best only if performance evaluations against the “strongest” attack fully captured the relative performance against the weaker attacks. This is not the case as shown in our evaluations.

> It highlights the very fact that improving performance on a “stronger” attack is not in general synonymous with improving performance on the “weaker” attacks.

I agree that some defenses can be better or worse against weak attacks even if they perform similarly against strong attacks. However, I think the adversarial robustness community has mostly decided that better performance against weak attacks is not useful. This is why nobody evaluates against FGSM any more! (or against DeepFool, C&W, etc. for the SOTA results on the top of the RobustBench leaderboard.) If an attacker can choose between a weaker attack or a stronger attack, why would they choose the weaker one? The only reasonable answer is it might be computationally less expensive. However, given that an attacker might only need to attack a few inputs to cause harm, there is little reason to believe they would need to use a weaker attack for computational reasons. Even the most computationally intensive attack in your evaluation (AutoAttack) still takes only a couple minutes at most to generate an adversarial example.

In contrast, there is reason to believe that an attack would want to use a smaller or larger perturbation radius, or different $p$-norms, since these actually trade off between whether the attack will be perceptible and whether it will succeed. That is why I think these are more interesting variations of "unseen" attacks.

> We believe C&W is indeed breaking the L2 PGD-based defense... evaluating it on CW L2 attacks where out of bound candidates are rejected... the model only achieves 12.4% accuracy.

Are you counting the "rejected" candidates as failures of the attack, e.g. successes for the defense? This seems like the correct evaluation strategy, since C&W aims to find the closest adversarial example to the original input. If none can be found with the bound, then the attack has failed and it should be counted as a success for the defense. What is the accuracy of the PGD defense under this evaluation metric?

> We wanted to illustrate variability between potentially seen and unseen tunings of the same attack. We could add an additional AutoAttack evaluation indeed, although since AutoAttack is always unseen, it would not illustrate that point.

This seems reasonable, although it would probably be good to add AutoAttack as well re: my first comment.

content.title: Part 2/2 of initial reply
content.comment:
> The Max method from Tramèr and Boneh. I know MSD is supposedly better than Max, but this was only evaluated against the attack norms seen during training in Maini et al. It's possible Max does better than MSD against unseen attacks.

Tables 3 and 4 of Maini et al. do evaluate on many individual attacks that were not seen during training https://arxiv.org/pdf/1909.04068.pdf. Note that Maini et al. find on CIFAR10 that Avg performs significantly better than Max. Moreover, as stated by the reviewer, on both MNIST and CIFAR10, Maini et al find that MSD performs better than both Avg and Max anyway, so improving on MSD with REx suggests that MSD+REx would outperform Max on both datasets. 

However, a significant difference with Maini is that we use different tunings for some attacks, and as evidenced by several reviewers asking for it, it would be valuable to readers of the paper that we add this baseline.

> Perceptual Adversarial Training [1], which was designed to transfer to novel threat models.

We thank the reviewer for pointing us to this paper. While the use of specific attacks and tunings is very common and methodologically appealing, we believe, like the authors of PAT, that attackers are free not to constrain themselves to the usual methodology as long as attacks are successful. Therefore, we will set to evaluating a Perceptual Adversarial Robustness model on our benchmarks, and conversely, evaluating our models on the threat model described in that paper.

>  I was a bit disappointed that the authors didn't provide code for review but they do promise it when the paper is published.

We apologise for this; reproducibility is extremely important especially for work related to robustness. The code is now available as supplementary material. Training is done with the relevant .py files, testing with the notebooks to allow for more flexibility and tests. We will clean up the code (specifically, removing commented out code and splitting function definitions into a utils file) for the final code release.

content.title: Thank you
content.comment:
We thank all reviewers for their comments and suggestions.

**Improvements we will work on for the next iteration:**
1. Perceptual adversarial training: we will be adding it as a baseline.
2. Explaining distributional shifts and domain generalisation: it will be valuable for readers that we give more explanations on distributional shifts and domain generalisation. Several reviewers have given very valuable suggestions for relevant additions, such as giving explanations for why different attacks or tunings would generally (*generally* in the mathematical sense) represent different shifts.
3. We will consider adding another AutoAttack evaluation with a different $\epsilon$ to investigate the effect of REx for fixed norm but different radii.


**Why weak attacks:**
A common question in the last round of replies from reviewers has been "why evaluate on weaker attacks". It is a question that merits a clarification (perhaps even in the paper/appendix): weak attacks capture a signal that would be missed otherwise. Indeed, as argued in the discussion of our results, REx does improve significantly robustness against strong attacks and even unbounded attacks (which can't be ignored in the general context of robustness until out-of-distribution detectors are perfectly able to capture shifts beyond the typical $\epsilon$ balls); however, REx often lowers the accuracy slightly on the weakest attacks. In other words, weak attacks allow us to capture a trade-off in using REx, which is important information for readers. Not having those evaluations would suggest that REx is an improvement on every attack.


**Max method:**
As indicated in our replies to the reviewers, the Max method has already been shown by Maini et al. to have worse performance than MSD on the same datasets as us, and the same model for CIFAR10. Additionally, Max actually was shown to perform worse on CIFAR10 with a ResNet18 than Avg. *Therefore, as a final question to reviewers: in light of this, do reviewers feel that adding a Max evaluation would be worth it, or would explicitly referring to Table 3 and 4 in Maini et al. be sufficient for readers?*


We thank again the reviewers for helping us improve our manuscript, and will proceed to withdrawing the paper in the coming days.
